We design the expanding graph covers to admit many common classical codewords, which yield logical operators whose pairings select the logical CCZ gates independently. Without the product expansion assumption, the graph covers also yield classical LDPC codes over a fixed field with almost linear dimension and linear distance that satisfy a multiplication property: the coordinatewise product of any three codewords lies in a second LDPC code of linear distance.

title: Analytical Interacting Tight-binding Model for Fractional Chern Insulators
summary: We construct a two-dimensional 2-band tight-binding model with two-body interactions and without magnetic lattice translation, in which both the hopping and interaction are exponentially local (with Gaussian decay) in real space. The interaction is built from pair annihilation operators whose coefficients are hopping amplitudes divided by positive powers of relative distance. Without any band projection, the ground states at $1/3$ filling are exactly fractional Chern insulator (FCI) states (and thus have nonzero gap) for any finite lattice size with any periodic/twist boundary conditions. The FCI ground states are analogous to the discretized version of the Laughlin-like states in the continuum Chern-ideal band, though our FCI states do not require the onsite spinor structure that is necessary in the continuum. We further show analytically that, after adding one unit cell while keeping electron number fixed, the anyonic one-quasihole states are zero-energy ground states of the full Hamiltonian for any finite system size and any quasihole position, analogous to Laughlin quasiholes under the Haldane $V_1$ pseudopotential. Numerical evidence is provided for the possible nonzero gap of the FCI states at $1/3$ filling in the thermodynamic limit, when interaction strength is much smaller than the single-particle band gap.

title: Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite Qubit System
comment: Keywords: Qubit, forsterite, quantum gates, Fe$^{2+}$, zero-field splitting (ZFS), two-level system
summary: Quantum Computing uses quantum mechanical phenomena, such as superposition and entanglement of quantum bits (qubits), to represent and manipulate information in multidimensional state spaces. This approach allows complex mathematical functions to be executed simultaneously rather than sequentially, making them much more efficient than classical computers. However, current quantum computers suffer from quantum decoherence, where small changes to their environment, such as thermal fluctuations and vibrations, affect the systems' fragile states. The goal of this study is to discuss the functionality of a proposed Fe$^{2+}$:forsterite qubit system by solving the unitary time-evolution of a quantum state vector for the system's Hamiltonian, using known axial and traverse anisotropy terms at temperatures up to 10 K. The system can effectively transfer population between its two lowest states at rates predicted by the Rabi half-period, with 99.9% fidelity. Additionally, it can hold the population at a desired state without docohering. The results remained consistent for temperatures up to 10 K, meaning, unlike many common qubit systems, the proposed qubit system could function without a dilution fridge and is not fragile to thermal noise.

title: A Bose-Hubbard quantum thermal machine
summary: This work proposes a quantum thermal machine comprised of interacting ultracold bosons confined in a one-dimensional optical lattice and modeled by the Bose-Hubbard Hamiltonian. We consider an Otto-inspired cycle with strokes that change the interaction strength between bosons, in addition to standard thermalization and compression/expansion strokes. We find that these interaction changes can be manipulated to enhance the performance of the thermal machine, outperforming non-interacting cycles. In particular, when operating as a heat engine, the cycle can achieve its largest work output and near-Carnot efficiency by compressing the medium at strong repulsion into a Mott insulator state. Additionally, we find that decreasing interactions after the compression stroke favors and enhances the engine operation, whereas increasing interactions favors refrigeration cycles. The findings of this work further show that controlling the interactions across quantum phases of matter can be harnessed as a useful thermodynamic resource.

title: Non-Abelian Hall Effects of Flavor-Waves in $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ Skyrmions
summary: We investigate the collective excitations of isolated and crystalline $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ skyrmions in a two-dimensional triangular-lattice spin-1 magnet. In a uniform spin-polarized state, these flavors can be identified with single-spin-flip and double-spin-flip excitations, whereas a nonuniform $\mathbb{CP}^{2}$ texture mixes their character. We formulate the corresponding bosonic Bogoliubov--de Gennes problem and examine the matrix-valued gauge connection governing flavor-wave propagation. For isolated skyrmions, the calculated spectrum contains localized modes, and the scattering dynamics exhibit transverse deflection accompanied by isospin precession. For a numerically relaxed skyrmion crystal, we obtain collective-mode bands with nonzero Chern numbers and calculate the associated thermal Hall response. These findings illustrate how projective magnetic textures couple multipolar excitations to non-Abelian transport and topological band phenomena.

title: Hierarchical coupling in tripartite van der Waals cavity magnonics for a low-loss and tunable coupled-mode Hamiltonian
summary: One of the greatest merits of cavity magnonics (CM) is the ability to explore rich coupled-mode physics, driven by the large \textit{in situ} flux tunability of magnonic resonances and magnon--photon coupling. summary: Spectral bounds for Markov generators require a choice of time scale. In quantum dynamics, a rate read off from a jump representation, the escape rate from a pure state and the smallest spectral disk need not agree. This settles the first two scaling conjectures of "Corralling spectra of generators of time-continuous Markov evolution (both classical and quantum)", J. Phys. A: Math. Theor. {59}, 175202 (2026). The third, escape-rate conjecture fails for a qutrit with a single normal jump. Nevertheless, twice the escape rate bounds every decay rate of any positive trace-preserving semigroup For GKLS generators with vanishing canonical Hamiltonian, four times the escape rate always supplies a spectral disk, and the factor four is optimal uniformly in dimension. summary: Out-of-time-order correlators (OTOCs) are quantities of broad interest in many-body physics due to their connection with information scrambling and quantum chaos. Recently, estimating higher-order OTOCs in random quantum circuits was proposed as a promising avenue for quantum advantage, yet the classical hardness of this task remains poorly understood. In this work, we introduce "window propagation," the first provably polynomial-time classical algorithm for approximating first-order OTOCs in 1D Haar-random brickwork circuits, at arbitrary depths and with inverse-polynomial mean-squared error. We also conduct numerical experiments comparing our simulation results to exact computation on up to $512$ qubits for Clifford circuits with $768$ $T$-gates and up to $22$ qubits for Haar-random circuits. We emphasize that our results do not directly apply to second-order OTOCs in 2D, which is the subject of recent quantum advantage proposals. Nevertheless, our work provides a rigorous step towards understanding the classical complexity of OTOC estimation and represents a family of non-trivial quantum circuits for which a provable, polynomial time algorithm is now known, establishing foundations for understanding these widely used diagnostics of quantum chaos.

title: Gutzwiller Quantum-Classical Embedding for Dynamics Simulations of Correlated Electron Systems
summary: Simulating the real-time dynamics of correlated electron systems requires a nonperturbative treatment of local correlations over long times, a challenge for classical methods. Within the time-dependent ghost Gutzwiller approximation, the lattice dynamics is mapped onto a noninteracting quasiparticle lattice, propagated classically, coupled to finite interacting embedding models propagated on quantum processors. The two parts exchange only embedding Hamiltonian parameters and single-particle density matrices, and the framework is agnostic to the quantum dynamics solver. We demonstrate it with adaptive variational quantum dynamics simulations of interaction quenches in the Hubbard model on the Bethe lattice. Without ghost orbitals, the embedding problem reduces to a single qubit, simulated on IBM quantum hardware with two qubits, including an ancilla. With more ghost orbitals, t-GQCE suppresses the artificial undamped oscillations of the conventional Gutzwiller approximation and approaches nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory results for weak and strong quenches. Statevector simulations with 2, 4 and 6 ghost orbitals per spin, or 8, 12 and 16 qubits, give adaptive circuits that follow the embedding states with infidelities below $5\times10^{-4}$. Under trapped-ion noise models, circuit compression, measurements in rotated orbital bases with post-selection, and noise mitigation reduce the measurement errors severalfold. At one third of the error rates of a hardware-benchmarked noise model, they reach an accuracy of $0.01$ for the single-particle density matrix and the double occupancy with $10^5$ shots per time step, and the Quantinuum H2-Emulator gives similar accuracy.

title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
summary: Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.

title: Instrument indeterminacy: separating uncertainty in POVM effects and its neutrosophic reading
summary: Neutrosophic annotation frameworks for quantum measurement attach an external triple $(t,i,f)$ to each Born probability, and explicitly leave open how indeterminacy could be defined operationally. We show that indeterminacy cannot be recovered from outcome probabilities, but can be computed from the pair (state, effect). For a binary POVM $\{A, I-A\}$ we define the instrument indeterminacy $\mathcal{I}_ρ(A) = 4 \mathrm{Tr}(ρ(A-A^2))$, which vanishes exactly when the state only sees the sharp part of the effect. The normalized Gini index of the outcome splits as $4TF = \mathcal{I}_ρ(A) + 4 \mathrm{Var}_ρ(A)$, a law of total variance that separates the instrument contribution from the state contribution; the identity is a special case of Massar's POVM uncertainty operator, and our contribution is its neutrosophic reading. Moving the system-apparatus cut to a Naimark dilation transfers exactly $\mathcal{I}_ρ(A)$ from indeterminacy to variance, which yields the missing operational definition. We extend the decomposition to $m$-outcome POVMs, relate the minimum indeterminacy of two incompatible unbiased qubit observables to their commutator through Busch's joint-measurability criterion, and show that $\mathcal{I}_ρ(A)$ equals twice the disagreement probability of a repeated Lüders measurement. The resulting estimator needs neither the state nor the effect and, in simulation, requires 2.5 to 6 times fewer shots than detector tomography for the same error.

title: A Nonsecular Quantum Master Equation with Detailed Balance and Second-order Error Bound
summary: An effective theory of open quantum systems should preserve the detailed balance structure inherited from microscopic reversibility and remain accurate throughout relaxation. Meeting both requirements is particularly challenging in quantum many-body systems, where dense spectra can invalidate the secular approximation even at weak coupling. Here we construct a nonsecular quantum master equation that satisfies time-reversal Kubo-Martin-Schwinger (TR-KMS) detailed balance. Under suitable conditions, we prove a time-uniform $O(λ^2)$ bound on the difference between the predicted and exact reduced density matrices, where $λ$ is the system-bath coupling strength. Our construction completes the Redfield generator by imposing detailed balance while matching its dissipative and coherent coefficients at resonance. In this approach, TR-KMS detailed balance is compatible with resonance matching, whereas its counterpart without time reversal is not. In a benchmark against the exact microscopic dynamics of two coupled oscillators, our equation maintains $O(λ^2)$ accuracy across secular and nonsecular regimes, outperforming the existing detailed-balance equations tested. These results provide a systematic route from microscopic models to thermodynamically consistent descriptions of open quantum dynamics beyond the secular approximation.

title: The magical memory cost of entanglement spectrum compression
summary: How much quantum memory is needed to faithfully retain the entanglement spectrum of a bipartite pure state after separating out Bell pairs through local unitaries? Smoothed entanglement spread bounds this memory cost from below, while diverging nonlocal magic forces unbounded memory at any fixed positive fidelity. Chaotic circuit dynamics exhibit a transient memory peak whose height increases with system size, followed by declining cost despite continued entropy growth. A large typical Haar-random state requires only an accuracy-dependent memory, whereas stationary fermionic Gaussian states retain a growing cost with size. In the circuits studied, the multiscale spectral structure associated with entanglement catalysis also has a practical consequence for matrix product state compression, yielding a multiplicative overhead not captured by the conventional entropy-based bond dimension estimate.

title: Exact Parent Hamiltonians for Partially Magnetized Chiral Spin Liquids
summary: Chiral spin liquids (CSLs) are paradigmatic fractionalized phases, yet simple exact parent Hamiltonians for them remain scarce. In this work, we construct exact spin parent Hamiltonians for partially magnetized CSLs realizing various bosonic topological orders. Our construction relies on an exact Hubbard-type parent Hamiltonian for bosonic lattice fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states, valid at arbitrary repulsive interaction strengths. Taking the on-site repulsion to infinity and applying local boson-spin mappings yields exact parent Hamiltonians for the CSLs. Our two-spin construction generalizes the Kalmeyer-Laughlin spin Hamiltonian to a broader class of bosonic FQH model states, including Abelian states and non-Abelian parton states. We derive controlled microscopic realizations of these two-spin Hamiltonians via second-order superexchange in generalized spinful Hofstadter-Hubbard models with tailored hoppings and interactions. With more general local constraints and interactions, boson-spin mappings yield exact higher-spin and multispin parent Hamiltonians for partially magnetized CSLs.

title: Perspectives on the hidden subgroup problem over unitriangular groups
summary: We investigate the quantum Hidden Subgroup Problem (HSP) over the upper unitriangular group $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$. While efficient quantum algorithms were discovered for some families of non abelian groups and nil-2 $p$-groups, no efficient algorithms are known for groups of nilpotency class higher than 2. The only techniques known for such groups scale exponentially in the size of the input. We first study the group $U_4(\mathbb{F}_p)$, the smallest upper unitriangular group exhibiting nilpotency class three. We analyze the application of the Pretty Good Measurement approach used for Heisenberg groups and show its limits. We then focus on the more general case $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$ to adapt existing techniques to this particular structure. In particular, we derive an algorithm for cyclic subgroups as a subroutine for a general algorithm, although it is not efficient in the size of the group. Our results highlight the difficulties introduced by the increasing nilpotency class and suggests some directions for an efficient quantum algorithm for the HSP over $U_n(\mathbb{F}_p)$.

title: Uniformly Convergent Perturbation Theory for Open Quantum Systems at, near, and away from Exceptional Points
summary: Near a Liouvillian exceptional point, spectral perturbation theory becomes ill-conditioned, yet the observable dynamics of a finite-dimensional open system remains regular in the perturbation. Using a Dyson expansion, which requires no diagonalization of the perturbed generator, we analyze the scaling, stability, and convergence of the perturbative corrections at, near and away from exceptional points. We derive scaling laws showing that nonperipheral Jordan blocks raise the degree of the polynomial-in-time factors multiplying decaying exponentials, which are present for any generator as resonances, and we quantify this excess. We further establish a uniform-in-time error estimate for the perturbative series, valid for any relaxing finite-dimensional Lindbladian and controlled by a parameter $q = |\varepsilon|R$, where $\varepsilon$ is the perturbation strength and $R$ is a constant built from unperturbed data. All constants of the bound remain continuous through an exceptional point when the coalescing eigenvalues are kept in one spectral cluster. The estimate extends to the frequency domain via the Laplace transform, and to time-dependent perturbations. We test it in a driven two-level system with a Liouvillian exceptional point, including perturbations that break its symmetry.

title: Parisi Energy before Parisi Geometry in the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures, supplemental material included (45 pages, 10 figures)
summary: The fractured low-energy landscape of spin glasses presents a notorious barrier to optimization. While high-depth calculations indicate that the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) can approach the Parisi ground-state energy of the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass, how it does so remains elusive. We draw two independent bitstrings from the same problem instance and couple them through their macroscopic similarity. We find that typical QAOA samples remain macroscopically uncorrelated, even as their sensitivity to this coupling grows with circuit depth $p$. By contrast, the low-energy tail shows a much stronger tendency to overlap and reveals a Parisi-like phase with the same critical behavior as the thermal spin-glass transition. The onset of this organization moves toward the typical output as the circuit deepens, consistent with the separation vanishing only as $p\to\infty$. Together, these findings suggest a route distinct from structure-exploiting classical algorithms and thermal sampling, one in which the QAOA approaches the Parisi energy before Parisi geometry becomes typical.

title: Renormalization and exact Bloch bands: the trigonometric Rosen-Morse model
summary: We study the trigonometric Rosen-Morse potential as an isolated singular well and as an exactly solvable periodic lattice. The potential combines inverse-square singularities with Coulomb terms of opposite signs. In the strongly attractive regime, independent renormalization at the two endpoints gives a two-parameter family of spectra. Deep negative-energy levels form two asymptotic sequences with the same Efimov-like scaling and opposite first-order Coulomb corrections. In the weak-medium regime, self-adjoint matching conditions allow transmission between neighboring cells. We obtain the exact Bloch dispersion relation and determine the band widths, gaps, and electron and hole effective masses. At fixed band index, the bandwidth becomes exponentially small in the limit of large Coulomb coupling.

title: Separating QMA from the QCMA Hierarchy via a Switching Lemma for Polynomials
summary: We construct a classical oracle relative to which QMA is not contained in the QCMA hierarchy. Our main technical contribution is a switching lemma for bounded polynomials, which provides a new conceptual viewpoint on earlier sampler-based arguments separating QMA and QCMA. Crucially, the parameters of this switching lemma are independent of the number of input variables. The separation builds on the code intersection subset size problem of Bostanci, Huang, and Vaikuntanathan (FOCS 2026). We also construct a classical oracle relative to which QCMA collapses to P but QMA does not, and another relative to which QMA collapses to P but PP does not.

summary: Resonantly driven two-level quantum batteries (QBs) suffer from strong pulse-area dependence and energy backflow inherent to Rabi oscillations. We show that sufficiently strong chirp modulation converts the charging mechanism from pulse-area-governed Rabi rotation to adiabatic rapid passage. We analyze the underlying adiabatic dynamics and derive the criteria for robust chirped charging, which incorporate the sweep bandwidth, nonadiabatic transitions, and dissipative effects. Under strong chirp modulation, the final stored energy and ergotropy converge to stable plateaus that are nearly insensitive to the pulse area across an extended parameter window. Of the four schemes, the sech pulse with tanh chirp delivers the widest ergotropy plateau and the weakest pulse area sensitivity. Compared with counterdiabatic driving, the sech tanh protocol attains stable charging performance without demanding an extra drive quadrature. Furthermore, this chirp-enabled charging is resilient to static detuning and weak-to-moderate dissipation. This work establishes a practical route toward robust charging of quantum batteries using chirped pulse control.

title: Parity Push Post-Selection with Soft Parity Constraints for Quantum LDPC Codes
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables; Supplementary Information: 9 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables
summary: Post-selection lowers the logical error rate of a quantum error-correcting code by rejecting unreliable shots. Each push adds one check node and one variable node to the Tanner graph of the detector error model, and we accept a shot only when every re-decoding returns a solution in the original logical class. We show that, with degenerate maximum-likelihood decoding, PPPS accepts a shot exactly when the logical gap exceeds the push strength $λ$. Applied with the Relay-BP decoder to the [[72,12,6]] bivariate bicycle code at $p=10^{-3}$ and the [[144,12,12]] code at $p=3\times10^{-3}$ under circuit-level depolarizing noise, PPPS lowers the logical error rate by factors of about 50 and 75, respectively, at rejection rates near 1%. We observe that PPPS rejects failures that prior post-selection strategies cannot reject, and thus shows improved performance.

title: Subsystem evolution in the history state formalism
summary: We present a relational framework for characterizing the evolution of quantum composite systems, based on the correlations within a history state describing the whole evolution relative to a quantum reference clock. While total system-clock entanglement entropy consistently measures the unitary evolution of the closed global system, a different picture emerges for the reduced state of an open subsystem, whose evolution is generally non-unitary due to environmental coupling. We introduce a general formalism that quantifies open-subsystem dynamics using a subsystem-clock mutual information derived from the history state. We demonstrate that this quantity serves as a consistent quantifier of subsystem evolution with respect to a given clock basis, can be applied to arbitrary dynamics, and reduces to system-time entanglement entropy in the global limit. Furthermore, maximizing this measure over all clock bases yields a basis-independent bound on the maximum evolution achievable relative to the clock, directly linked to the difference between the subsystem's entanglement with the rest of the history state and its entanglement with the environment. Finally, we derive analytical expressions for qubit clocks, illustrate our results using spin 1/2 and spin 1 quantum walks, and present a full matrix formalism of Kraus operators for describing the most general subsystem evolution.

title: QWeaver: Quantum Circuit Cut Workflow with MLIR-based Compiler, Runtime, and Weaver Hybrid Tasks
comment: This is the pre-print version of the article to appear in SN Computer Science. Code will be released once manuscript is published
summary: Quantum computers available today are constrained by limited qubit counts and high noise levels, making the direct execution of large quantum circuits infeasible on a single device, and while quantum circuit cutting addresses this by partitioning a large circuit into smaller subcircuits for independent execution, orchestrating the full end-to-end workflow remains a significant programming challenge. In this paper, we present QWeaver, a task-graph-based programming and orchestration workflow framework for quantum circuit cutting that accepts OpenQASM quantum circuits as input and constructs a directed acyclic task graph. In this graph, the Multi-Level Intermediate Representation (MLIR)-based circuit cut is the first task, responsible for analyzing and partitioning the input circuit into executable fragment representations; the generated fragments are then handed to a set of quantum circuit execution tasks that depend on the cut task and can be dispatched concurrently across available quantum backends via the Quantum Intelligent Runtime System (Q-IRIS). Finally, a weaving task, dependent on all execution tasks, performs classical post-processing that applies quasi-probability reconstruction techniques to combine the sampled measurement outcomes of all fragments and recover an accurate approximation of the original circuit's output distribution. We describe the architecture of QWeaver, its integration with Q-IRIS and the execution engine for the Quantum Intermediate Representation (QIR-EE), validate end-to-end reconstruction on GHZ and Harris-Ross instances, and evaluate systems and width trade-offs on structured GHZ simulator workloads.

title: Spectral Engineering of Charge Localization and Work Reliability in Collective Quantum Batteries
summary: The performance of a quantum battery depends not only on how much energy it stores, but also on how rapidly useful charge can be restored after work extraction. We show how engineering the reservoir spectrum connects these properties in an interacting collective-spin battery. Interactions separate the Dicke transition frequencies, allowing frequency-selective pumping and loss to control where excitation accumulates and how populations move along the ladder. Analytical results relate the pump-to-loss ratio to charge localization, fluctuations, and extractable work. Two reservoirs producing the same mean charge can nevertheless exhibit markedly different localization and charging times. Under repeated extraction, finite-time recharging also generates correlations between successive work outputs. At matched mean work, these correlations can reverse the ordering of single-cycle and long-time fluctuations: a protocol with larger fluctuations in individual strokes can deliver more reliable accumulated work. An exact counting relation connects these statistics to net charging-energy transfer, while relaxation modes distinguish recovery of the stationary state from recovery of useful work. Finally, local dephasing redistributes population among collective-spin sectors, leading to an exact stationary symmetry-dilution law and a finite operating window for work extraction under a collective transverse controller.

title: Stationary Quantum Time Series: Spectral Theory of Process Memory and Measurement Records
summary: Classical time series analysis converts temporal dependence into structure that can be learned from a single observed trajectory, through stationarity, ergodicity, spectral representation, and finite-memory models. Quantum experiments are naturally time series: every run is a sequence of interventions and outcomes, and the memory of an open system is written in its temporal statistics. However, the classical foundation cannot be translated directly: measuring a process and forgetting the outcome differs from not measuring at all, so no single family of joint probability distributions describes a quantum process. We develop a process-tensor framework for stationary quantum time series and establish its first structural theorems. For stationary combs of finite quantum Markov order l relative to a fixed informationally complete causal break, we construct a finite-dimensional causal transfer map of dimension at most d^{4l}, where d bounds the system Hilbert-space dimension at each step. ... These results supply the stationary foundation on which quantum spectral analysis, model identification, and single-trajectory inference can be built.

title: Covering the Pauli Observables: Sampling Thresholds and the Design Effect of a Measurement Setting
summary: Quantum state tomography and shadow-based estimation rely on measuring Pauli observables. An experiment does not measure them one at a time: it chooses a measurement setting that assigns one of the bases X, Y or Z to each qubit, and a single run in that setting yields estimates of every Pauli observable compatible with it. We say that the setting covers those observables. We determine how many random settings cover a prescribed fraction of all Pauli observables. As the number of settings grows exponentially with the number of qubits, the covered fraction has a sharp threshold at a growth rate of $3^{3/4}$ per qubit, set by the rate-distortion function of covering at zero distortion. We give an explicit expression for the number of settings needed to reach a target fraction, accurate up to a remainder that reduces to a small oscillation for many qubits, and show that random sampling is asymptotically optimal up to a factor of less than 1.69. Coverage does not determine what a setting contributes to an estimator. Observables covered by one setting are estimated from the same outcomes, so their estimates are correlated. We quantify this correlation through the design effect of a setting, which equals the squared Pauli expectation that the setting captures and depends on the target state. We derive its mean over settings in closed form for every state and show that it can be estimated without bias from the measurement data. In simulations on six qubits, measuring settings needs 7.6 to 38 times fewer circuit runs than measuring the same number of observables independently. At high coverage, fitting the outcome histograms instead of averaged estimates roughly halves the reconstruction error, mainly because the fit counts how many settings cover each observable. The correlation itself costs such a fit about a factor of two, and a larger design effect signals more to gain from modeling it.

title: Aharonov-Bohm blockade of complete reversal in coupled Rabi cavities
summary: When a common bias reverses two bistable fields, the system can pass through either of two single-reversal configurations on its way to the favored state. We show that interference between these two orders of reversal can block the final step. In a dimer of coupled quantum Rabi cavities, the four field configurations form a loop, and a complex photon-hopping amplitude threads it with an Aharonov-Bohm flux. Near half a flux quantum, the two paths to complete reversal interfere destructively: in microscopic simulations, a slow uniform sweep reverses one field with probability 0.998, although the final bias favors reversing both. A four-state model calibrated at zero bias predicts how the window of this Aharonov-Bohm blockade narrows with sweep time. The blocked state remains coherent. A differential pulse followed by a return sweep converts the relative phase of the two single-reversal configurations into a fringe in the joint field signs, with contrast 0.95. In a trimer, a phase gradient imprinted between sweeps determines whether the next sweep adds or removes a reversed field: reversing the second of two gradients changes the most probable outcome from three reversed fields to one.

title: Imaging chiral snake states in a qubit array with programmable gauge fields
comment: 22 pages, 12 figures (4 main-text figures and 8 Extended Data figures), and 1 Extended Data table
summary: Spatially varying magnetic fields steer charged particles along directed paths. Where a field reverses sign, particles follow snake-like orbits along the reversal line, in a direction set by both the field orientation and the sign of their energy. Transport measurements have detected such snake states, but imaging their dynamics in a reprogrammable field landscape remains challenging. Here we digitally simulate the Harper--Hofstadter model with programmable synthetic magnetic fields on a 49-qubit superconducting processor. In each Trotter step, every hopping term is one native fractional-iSWAP gate, and single-qubit $Z$ rotations set all 36 plaquette fluxes independently, without additional entangling gates. Uniform, random, and stepped flux landscapes reveal Aharonov--Bohm suppression of diagonal propagation, disorder-induced slowing, and magnetic reflection. At a field reversal, bonding and antibonding initial states, which carry opposite energy biases, propagate in opposite directions, and both directions reverse when the field is inverted. A symmetry analysis of these reversals yields a chiral displacement of nearly one lattice spacing after ten Trotter rounds, with symmetry-breaking residuals below 0.05 lattice spacings. Bond-resolved flux programming with site-resolved imaging thus provides a quantitative tool for synthetic gauge fields and a route to time-dependent gauge fields and interacting particles.

title: Fault-tolerant quantum processor with minimal external control
comment: Reader's guide included at the end of section 1
summary: Contemporary classical information processors integrate tens of billions of transistors printed on a chip, yet are fully controlled through comparatively few external wires. This is possible because data flows through hard-coded operations in step with a global clock and is steered by external instructions. Today's solid-state quantum processors are different -- every qubit receives instructions from outside the chip via its own dedicated control line, and error correction adds a further torrent of syndrome data that is transported off-chip. Here we show that the external control of a quantum chip can be greatly simplified. We propose a fault-tolerant architecture for universal quantum computation, inspired by modern classical processors, in which quantum information flows through a fixed, clocked device, propelled by local gates in a planar array. Our quantum processor receives an input stream of classical instructions via a small, constant number of external wires, each attached to a single qubit. Except for those few qubits coupled to external wires, all qubits evolve under a periodically-applied geometrically-local depth-3 circuit, which is fixed at the time the device is fabricated. Assuming a noiseless global clock (so that every operation is applied on schedule, though imperfectly), we establish an accuracy threshold theorem: For physical noise below a universal threshold -- afflicting every gate, measurement, and wire -- a chip with $n$ physical qubits can run any quantum algorithm that uses~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/ε)$ logical qubits, where $ε$ is the error rate per logical gate. Each logical gate takes time~$n/{\sf polylog}(n/ε)$; an alternative design, in which quantum operations remain strictly local and noisy, but on-chip wires broadcast noiseless classical signals instantaneously, reduces the time per logical gate to ${\sf polylog}(n/ε)$.

title: General Noise Channels and Mid-Circuit Measurements for Pre-Trajectory Sampling with Batched Execution
comment: 25 pages, 8 figures (4 in the main text, 4 in the Supplementary Information)
summary: Many studies of quantum protocols require fast sampling of large amounts of measurement data from noisy quantum circuits, such as for training machine-learning decoders for quantum error correction. Exact simulation of realistic noise is expensive, while stabilizer-based simulators are fast but approximate, for example through Pauli twirling, which generally alters the output statistics. Pre-trajectory sampling with batched execution (PTSBE) accelerates exact trajectory simulation by sampling noise before state evolution. This method requires the outcome probability of every stochastic event to be independent of the state, which excludes mid-circuit measurements and general Kraus channels. We present a generalization of PTSBE to measurement and Kraus operators without approximation. Each event is partially pre-sampled, while deferred outcomes are drawn during grouped execution via multinomial branching and cached-state reuse. We implement the method for GPUs as an extension of CUDA-Q. On distance-3 topological code memories under amplitude damping, it is up to 24x faster than conventional trajectory sampling in CUDA-Q. On 30-qubit random circuits with mid-circuit measurements, it is up to 83x faster and outperforms the near-Clifford simulator Clifft when more than about 25% of the gates are non-Clifford. With repeated sampling of each final state, its sampling rate per trajectory exceeds that of CUDA-Q by nearly five orders of magnitude. Our method also allows us to compare exact amplitude damping with its Pauli-twirled channel on a surface-code memory, revealing that twirling overestimates the detection rate by 21% and raises the logical error rate of a lookup decoder by 8%. This work makes exact, high-throughput simulation practical for general noisy circuits, from data generation for training decoders to studying measurement-based fault-tolerant protocols under realistic noise.

title: Faster than square-root run-time in adiabatic quantum algorithms for Exact Cover 3
summary: By intertwining ideas from sequential and adiabatic quantum computing, we propose a quantum algorithm for the problem class Exact Cover 3, which is a sub-class of 3-satisfiability (3-SAT) problems and NP (nondeterministic polynomial time) complete. We find a quantum run-time which is significantly faster than the square-root run-time $N\to N^{1/2}$ of the Grover algorithm. Depending on the structure of the problem (e.g., connectivity of clauses), the run-time scaling may range from approximately third root $N\to N^{1/3}$ to nearly fourth root $N\to N^{1/4}$, possibly even faster.

title: Analysis of a Homodyne-Like Measurement Scheme Using Photon Counters and Weak Local Oscillator
summary: In standard homodyne detection, an unknown optical signal state is combined with a local oscillator (LO) at a beam splitter (BS), and the appropriately integrated intensities at the two outputs of the BS are subtracted to obtain an approximate quadrature measurement. Accurate quadrature measurements require a high-amplitude LO and high-efficiency detectors. By varying the LO phase, the optical state in the mode matching the LO can be reconstructed. In many practical settings, a high-intensity LO is not desirable, which has led to the exploration of homodyne-like measurement schemes that replace photodiodes with photon-counting detectors and use an LO with a low average photon number. In this paper, we investigate what features of the unknown state can be determined by counting the total-photon number in one or both outgoing paths after the BS, keeping the mode of the LO fixed but adjusting its phase and magnitude. We find that it is possible to determine the unknown optical state in the mode matching the LO conditional on the number of photons in the orthogonal modes on the same path. If both the phase and the intensity of the LO can be varied, the statistics of just one of the detectors is sufficient to infer these parameters, but both detectors are required when the LO has a fixed intensity. Our analysis is carried out in the infinite-data limit, assuming access to the full photon-number distribution from one or both detectors.

title: Quantum Mpemba effect in a driven-dissipative atom-waveguide coupled system
summary: The quantum Mpemba effect (QME) describes the counterintuitive phenomenon in which a more strongly perturbed quantum system relaxes toward its steady state faster than a less perturbed one. Here, we investigate the QME in a weakly driven-dissipative atomic array coupled to a one-dimensional chiral waveguide. Starting from the steady state, we introduce a local quench by resetting a single atom to its ground state and examine the subsequent relaxation dynamics. We find that quenching atoms near the array boundaries induces faster initial relaxation through enhanced coupling to superradiant modes and direct photon emission into the waveguide, giving rise to an edge-enhanced QME. Strong directional decay further amplifies this effect by promoting the spatial accumulation of superradiant modes near the preferred boundary, leading to a skin-enhanced QME. At later times, relaxation is increasingly governed by long-lived subradiant modes localized predominantly in the bulk of the array. By coupling two atomic arrays with different interparticle spacings, we further demonstrate an interface-induced QME, where quenching an atom near the interface makes the system relax more slowly at early times but approach its steady state faster at later times, owing to weak participation in both superradiant and subradiant modes. Our findings reveal how the spatial structure of collective decay modes and directional dissipation jointly govern anomalous quantum relaxation, offering potential routes toward accelerated steady-state preparation in waveguide QED systems.

title: Topological Origin of Directional Amplification in Arbitrary-Dimensional Non-Hermitian Lattices
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, with Supplemental Material (11 pages, 1 figure)
summary: In non-Hermitian lattices, combinations of gain, loss and nonreciprocal couplings can generate exponentially growing directional amplification with applications in signal processing and precision measurement. An intriguing question is whether such amplification has a universal topological origin in arbitrary dimensions. Here we establish a dimension-independent framework to uncover the topological origin of directional amplification based on the concept of amoeba, which is the logarithmic image of the singularities of the response generating function. The complement of the amoeba in the logarithmic parameter space consists of connected components, each carrying a distinct and discrete topological label. We show that the asymptotic response is governed by the component extending toward negative infinity. When the origin of the logarithmic parameter space is outside this component and not on its boundary, there must exist some directions in which the response is exponentially amplified. Otherwise, there is no directional amplification in any direction. Our results provide a general topological criterion for classifying the responses in arbitrary-dimensional non-Hermitian lattices.

title: Topological Quantum Reservoir Computing
summary: Scaling universal quantum computation and implementing quantum machine learning with protected logical qubits remain challenging. To harness the computational potential of existing fault-tolerant quantum platforms, we introduce topological quantum reservoir computing, a novel approach using protected degrees of freedom for storage and the host system's intrinsic dynamics for information processing. Using a one-dimensional Kitaev chain, we show how long-lived Majorana edge modes and fast bulk responses support these complementary functions within the same many-body system. We identify the tradeoffs governing access to protected memory and show how matched interfaces enable programmable writing and interactions enable autonomous information consolidation from the bulk to the edge. These mechanisms improve performance on tasks requiring long-term retention of temporal information. Our results establish topology as a new resource for quantum reservoir computing and open a route toward near-term quantum computing and quantum machine learning.

title: Distinguishing Conserved Quantum Sectors via Measurement Record Features
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures, with 23 pages of Supplemental Material
summary: Conservation laws partition the Hilbert space of a quantum system into invariant sectors that are often difficult to identify directly. Repeated measurements on an ancillary probe, however, generate a measurement record that provides information about the occupied sector. Here we develop a framework for identifying conserved sectors using a $(K+1)$-dimensional feature vector of record statistics, comprising the average outcome frequency and pair-outcome correlations up to $K$ measurement cycles apart. For fixed $K$, the feature vector can be evaluated at a cost linear in record length. In quantum non-demolition measurement models, the average outcome frequency suffices for accurate sector identification. For an interacting spin bath with nontrivial dynamics within each sector, incorporating temporal correlations between successive and more widely separated measurements into the record feature vector substantially improves classification fidelity. Our framework provides an efficient approach to conserved-sector identification and demonstrates the importance of temporal correlations in distinguishing the underlying sector dynamics.

title: Vanilla Adiabatic Quantum Optimization Can Have Subexponential Advantage
summary: We construct a family of objective functions $f \colon \{0,1\}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ for which vanilla adiabatic quantum optimization along $H(s) = -(1-s)\sum_{i=1}^n X_i + s\sum_x f(x)\lvert x\rangle\!\langle x\rvert$ finds the global minimizer in $\operatorname{poly}(n)$ time, whereas any classical algorithm requires $\exp(n^{Ω(1)})$ time to do so in the black-box model. Our result is achieved by replacing the linearization technique in an earlier work of Leng et al. (arXiv:2504.14841), which establishes a similar subexponential quantum speedup using a transverse field Ising mixer rather than $-\sum_{i=1}^n X_i$.

title: Accelerating Quantum Error Correction Simulations under Coherent Noise with Compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product States
comment: Main text (8 pages, 6 figures), supplement (16 pages, 7 figures)
summary: Reliable assessment of quantum error correction requires understanding how coherent errors affect logical performance. Although tensor networks naturally capture coherent interference, entanglement growth and large qubit counts make repeated sampling costly. Here we develop a compiled Clifford-Augmented Matrix Product State (CAMPS) framework that reuses Clifford transformations across shots, recycles qubits released by measurements, evolves a compressed residual state, and accelerates sampling through rotation fusion and compilation tailored to the MPS layout. Surface-code benchmarks under fixed-sign coherent noise yield accurate logical error estimates at small bond dimensions, while random-sign simulations up to distance $d=9$ and on the $[[72,12,6]]$ bivariate bicycle code match the Pauli-twirling approximation results. Compared with uncompiled CAMPS, compiled CAMPS converges at smaller bond dimensions and achieves order-of-magnitude sampling speedups at equal bond dimension, opening a scalable route to studying coherent error propagation in larger fault-tolerant circuits.

title: Odd-Even Effects on Liouvillian Spectra and Relaxation Dynamics in Boundary-Driven Spin Chains
summary: We investigate odd-even effects on Liouvillian spectra and relaxation dynamics in boundary-driven XY and cluster chains. With the bulk couplings and boundary dissipation rule fixed, the parity of chain length determines whether non-decaying oscillatory modes exist. Consequently, odd- and even-sized chains exhibit qualitatively different dynamical behaviors. We trace this mechanism to the coupling between bulk Majorana paths and the boundary jump operators. An isolated path supports undamped modes, and products of an even number of its Majorana operators span a non?decaying subspace of even operators. This structure yields nonzero purely imaginary eigenvalues of the Liouvillian and persistent contributions to bond correlations or magnetization after preparation in product states. The mechanism extends to cluster interactions of even range under a fixed boundary dissipation rule. The existence and frequencies of the persistent modes are independent of the magnitudes of the positive boundary dissipation rates. Our results unveil how chain parity controls the existence of persistent dynamics.

title: Reliability of quantum communication over erasure channels
summary: Quantum information can be reliably transmitted at rates below the quantum capacity with an error that vanishes as the number of channel uses grows. The reliability function characterizes the optimal exponential decay rate of this error. For quantum erasure channels with a prime input dimension, we determine the reliability function exactly at all positive communication rates below capacity that meet or exceed an explicit critical rate. Notably, stabilizer coding strategies attain this optimal reliability throughout this regime.

title: CCZ gate beyond the strong Rydberg-blockade regime
summary: We present a protocol for implementing a controlled-controlled-Z (CCZ) gate on a neutral-atom platform, employing three individually addressable atoms confined in a linear array of optical tweezers and operating under finite Rydberg-Rydberg interaction (RRI). The protocol combines successive excitation of the Rydberg atoms with analytically determined pulses and uses two Rydberg levels to access opposite-sign interaction shifts. We show two different paths to get the conditional phase in the target atom: a pair of target pulses with opposite phases and a single detuned target pulse followed by a local phase correction. We derive analytical expressions for the time-integrated Rydberg populations to calculate the associated decay errors and also evaluate gate performance through master-equation simulations. Numerical comparisons with a fast Rydberg-antiblockade (RAB)-based CCZ protocol show improved gate performance at larger interatomic separations within the parameter regime considered. Monte Carlo sampling further quantifies the sensitivity to thermally induced position fluctuations. These results identify the tradeoffs between gate duration, Rydberg-state exposure, and interaction sensitivity, providing an analytically specified route to native three-qubit phase gates beyond the strong-blockade regime.

title: Quantum Annealing with a Quantum Neural Network: Width of Annealing Matters
summary: Quantum annealing is a promising quantum algorithm for dealing with computationally hard optimization problems. Currently available hardware can implement the algorithm for a significant class of Hamiltonian problems. However, its performance is especially limited in discontinuous quantum phase transitions, where the energy gap shrinks exponentially with system size. In this paper, we introduce an extension of quantum annealing to a quantum neural network and study its performance in a number of prototypical optimization problems. In particular, we observe that already a random quantum annealing network of width W = 2 can exponentially reduce the number of evolution layers or depth of the annealing process in the quantum search problem. By tuning the network parameters the search problem can be solved with exponentially small errors by a quantum perceptron of depth L = 1 and width W = 2. The findings show that width of a quantum annealing network is critical to enhance the success probability of the algorithm by providing a larger and learnable evolution space for the annealing process.

title: Quantum Parallel Algorithm for Multivariate Trace Estimation with Applications
summary: Estimating multivariate traces Tr(A1A2......Ak) is a fundamental task arising across diverse fields. In this paper, We develop a quantum algorithm for this problem tailored to near-term quantum devices. We access matrices by preparing their vectorized states. This access mode yields a tensor-network representation of the multivariate trace, which in turn guides the design of a parallel algorithm. The resulting circuit has depth dominated solely by that of the input oracle and independent of the number of matrices k, at the cost of a qubit count scaling as Θ(k)-a trade-off between circuit depth and circuit size. Moreover, the circuit exhibits a simple modular structure that allows explicit distribution over O(k) devices. We further establish efficient preparation circuits for a broad range of matrix classes, demonstrating the wide applicability of our approach. we present two applications: spectral sum estimation and a quantum implementation of the classical Lanczos method. Both reduce the target problem to sums of multivariate traces, thereby avoiding the construction of matrix polynomial transformations and achieving two levels of parallelism. For certain matrix classes, the resulting algorithms reduce circuit depth by a factor equal to the degree of the approximating polynomial. The shallow circuit depth and distributed implementation make our algorithms particularly suitable for near-term devices.

title: Gradient Blindness in Adaptive Architecture Search for IQP Born Machines
summary: Instantaneous quantum polynomial (IQP) Born machines learn a probability distribution from data with a circuit of commuting gates that a classical computer trains at hundreds of qubits. Adaptive algorithms grow a sparse circuit from a small seed by adding in every round the candidate gates with the largest loss gradient. Such algorithms never add a candidate whose gradient vanishes, so the choice of seed decides which circuits they can reach. Here we show that a candidate gate has a nonzero gradient for some angles of the circuit exactly when its generator is the sum of an odd number of linearly independent generators already in the circuit. The common seed of one-qubit gates therefore never adds a gate on an even number of qubits, which exact gradients on 12 qubits confirm. A seed of one-qubit gates plus the edges of the Chow-Liu tree sees every candidate, and its circuits match the full circuits on 12 and 16 qubits with 10 to 13 percent of their parameters. At 484 qubits, a heredity pool keeps the search over higher-order gates feasible, and the circuits grown from this seed reach a lower test loss than the dense two-body circuit with 6 percent of its parameters, although the higher-order gates add no gain.

title: In-memory measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution
summary: Quantum memories offer to significantly extend the performance of quantum networks, but their complexity and limited performance at telecommunication wavelengths have so far hindered practical deployment. We propose a new memory-assisted measurement device independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD) protocol based on in-memory interference. Our approach leverages progress in atomic ensemble memories that enable the interference of a stationary matter qubit and a travelling photonic qubit inside a single quantum memory. We quantitatively evaluate the performance of this scheme against memoryless MDI-QKD and existing two-memory architectures, showing that it not only achieves superior secret key rates and surpasses the memoryless bound at substantially shorter distances, but also reduces hardware requirements by halving the number of memories and detectors. Our results further indicate that off resonant cascaded absorption (ORCA) memories are a particularly promising platform for implementing this protocol, and we outline a concrete design compatible with their capabilities. These findings demonstrate that in-memory interference provides a higher performance, and resource efficient route toward near term memory enhanced quantum secure communications.

title: Quantifying extractable imaginarity with qubit triangles
summary: Two qubit states with the same robustness of imaginarity can differ in the robustness attainable by real filtering on a successful outcome. We represent the input robustness $R$ and the largest conditional robustness $κ$ by the base of a right triangle and the slope of its hypotenuse, respectively. Twice the area, $R^2κ$, defines a faithful, convex measure that is monotone on average under real instruments. In arbitrary finite dimensions, maximizing the mean normalized area of the extracted qubits gives the pointwise smallest strongly monotone extension of the qubit measure. We derive computable bounds on this area by determining the maximum mean squared robustness of the output qubits. This maximum equals the Bures quantum $χ^2$ divergence between the input and its real part. A projection onto orthogonal real subspaces attains the maximum and, when its outcome is retained, preserves the quantum Fisher information at the midpoint of a mixture of the input and its complex conjugate. We obtain exact areas for states with commuting real and imaginary parts and for pure states mixed with white noise. Two eight-dimensional states have identical $R$, $κ$, and optimal mean squared robustness, yet their different areas rule out deterministic conversion by real operations in one direction.

title: A Convex-Roof Affinity-Square Measure of Quantum Imaginarity
summary: Quantum imaginarity characterizes the part of a quantum state that cannot be represented by real density matrices in a fixed reference basis. We study an affinity-square measure of imaginarity for pure states and its convex-roof extension to mixed states. The pure state quantity is defined by minimizing the affinity-square measure over the convex set of real states. This optimization admits a closed expression determined by the modulus of the conjugation overlap between a state and its complex conjugate. The measure vanishes precisely when the state is real up to a global phase. We prove that the convex-roof extension is faithful, convex, monotone under real operations, and nonincreasing on average under selective real operations. For arbitrary single-qubit mixed states, we evaluate the convex roof exactly and express it in terms of the imaginary component of the off-diagonal density-matrix element. We also compare pure-state imaginarity with an auxiliary affinity-square coherence functional and give the corresponding phase weights.

title: QuFrame: Pauli Frame Tracking for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Control
summary:
Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires continuous quantum error correction (QEC) to suppress physical noise. While Clifford-only workloads can defer corrections to software post-processing, universal computation breaks this paradigm: executing non-Clifford gates via magic-state gadgets introduces hard, real-time control-flow dependencies on error-corrected measurements. Consequently, the controller must extract syndromes, decode them, and update the Pauli frame in real time, closing the entire QEC loop within a strict $1\,μ\text{s}$ cycle. However, prior proposals on Pauli frame tracking remain largely theoretical, leaving the microarchitectural bottlenecks of tracking, resolving, and synchronizing frame updates across distributed control pipelines unaddressed.
  To this end, we present QuFrame, a control microarchitecture for real-time Pauli frame tracking that closes the QEC loop within $1\,μ\text{s}$ while sustaining QPU-rate throughput. By introducing QuFrameISA, we cleanly decouple instruction execution from continuous Pauli frame management. Execution is distributed across per-qubit Instruction Resolution Engines (IREs) that resolve instructions against the frame via a single table lookup, while a Pauli Frame Management Unit enables independent, lock-free concurrent commits. To strictly guarantee the $1\,μ\text{s}$ deadline, QuFrame pairs an asynchronous primary decoder with an on-chip fallback decoder that resolves in $144\,\text{ns}$, natively reconciling divergent updates in hardware without degrading logical error rates.

title: Doppler effect on dual-downlink time-bin quantum key distribution and a proposed ephemeris-assisted witness-field correction
summary: Time-bin entanglement is promising for satellite Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) due to its compatibility with telecom fiber networks, but its phase-sensitive measurements are vulnerable to Doppler effects induced by satellite motion. We present a spectral-temporal framework for time-bin-entangled photon pairs generated onboard a satellite via Spontaneous Parametric Down Conversion (SPDC) and distributed to two Optical Ground Stations (OGSs) over independent downlinks with distinct Doppler shifts. Each OGS is equipped with an Unbalanced Mach-Zehnder Interferometer (UMZI) used to perform Bennett-Brassard-Mermin 1992 (BBM92) entangled-photon QKD. In a simulated Low Earth Orbit (LEO) pass with matched 400 ps analyzer delays, the received time-bin separation changes by at most 8.8 fs per link, while the combined carrier phase shifts by about 38 rad, which primarily degrades phase-basis correlations. After zero-Doppler calibration, this phase separates into independent signal-and idler-link contributions, allowing each station to correct its link Doppler phase shift locally, without real-time phase exchange between the stations. We propose an ephemeris-assisted feed-forward architecture, in which an auxiliary interferometer analyzes a co-propagating classical witness field to reconstruct the local Doppler-induced phase, which a phase modulator then compensates on the quantum channel. In a noise-free model, a 1 Hz sample-and-hold correction rate keeps the phase-basis Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) below 2% and retains 93% of the ideal asymptotic key yield. After 18 accumulated passes, the corrected finite secret key reaches 95% of its ideal length, whereas relabeling the parity from the ephemeris without optical correction reaches only about 8%.

title: Long-distance continuous variable entanglement distribution over deployed fibre
summary: Continuous-variable (CV) entanglement offers deterministic generation and room-temperature coherent detection for quantum networks, but distributing it over deployed fibre has been hindered by the need to stabilise optical phase, polarisation, and timing at remote receivers. Here we demonstrate, to our knowledge, the first distribution of CV entanglement over deployed metropolitan fibre using independent coherent receivers. The two modes of a two-mode squeezed vacuum state are delivered to remote nodes through 23 km ($\approx 7$ dB loss) and 450 m ($\approx 1$ dB loss) deployed fibre links. Each node uses its own free-running laser and polarisation-diverse coherent receiver. Co-propagating pilot tones enable digital recovery of timing, phase and polarisation, while inter-mode correlations fix the quadrature alignment. We certify entanglement with a Simon-Duan value of $1.915\pm 0.013$, below the separability bound of 2 and a logarithmic negativity of $0.067\pm0.011$. By replacing optical stabilisation with digital reconstruction, our approach offers a practical route towards scalable CV quantum networks.

title: Efficient simulation of variational quantum circuits: representation, accuracy and CPU/GPU allocation
summary: Classical circuit simulation supports quantum software development and verification and provides a baseline for assessing quantum advantage. We compare gate-based statevector simulation, direct Pauli evolution and matrix product states for molecular and spin Variational Hamiltonian Ansatze and hardware-efficient ansatze on CPU/GPU systems, varying width, depth, precision and resource allocation. In the tested implementations, direct Pauli evolution benefits complex molecular VHA, whereas GPUs accelerate wider spin and hardware efficient circuits. Matrix product state is useful when limited entanglement permits accurate compression; corrected CPU FP32 can meet the tested tolerance while costing more than FP64. Workload size, startup, worker memory and task-specific profiling can change the preferred allocation. Matched NumPy Pauli updates accelerate two-layer full LiH by 3.45-fold; the GPU gives approximately 30-fold acceleration over 18-thread Aer for 28-qubit, four-layer TFIM, both in FP64. We provide a procedure for choosing representation, precision and worker allocation jointly, comparing the cost of complete energy evaluations under accuracy, memory and core constraints.

title: A unified approach to the time-dependent quantum harmonic oscillator via point transformations and Lie symmetries
summary: We revisit the time-dependent harmonic oscillator (TDHO) in quantum mechanics based on the notion of equivalence transformations and Lie point symmetries. Within this framework, we give the most general point transformations depending on seven parameters which map from the TDHO to the usual harmonic oscillator (HO) and the other way around. As a byproduct we reconstruct the Schrödinger propagator (Mehler's kernel) for the time-independent harmonic oscillator. We demonstrate, without recourse to the Lewis--Riesenwert (LR) invariant, how Lie algebraic methods enable alternative derivation of the normalized wave functions of the TDHO by constructing solutions invariant under some specific subgroup of $\SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ combined with the gauge group. We further show that, on the relevant $\SL(2,\mathbb{R})$-invariant solution family, the Lewis--Riesenfeld operator defines a compatible second-order differential constraint, thereby clarifying its relation to the Lie symmetry structure of the TDHO.

title: Virtual Autopurification in Translationally Invariant Quantum States
summary: We introduce virtual autopurification (VAP), a protocol for virtual purification that operates entirely within a single translationally invariant system. Virtual purification suppresses thermal fluctuations and decoherence noise by amplifying the dominant pure component of a mixed state, but its standard implementation requires multiple copies of the state and global entangled measurements. VAP avoids the multiple-copy overhead by constructing virtual copies from spatially separated subregions and performing entangled measurements only between them. Assuming clustering of correlations, we show that VAP reproduces the expectation values of the standard virtual purification protocol, with discrepancies that decay exponentially in both the buffer length and the inter-subregion distance. Numerical simulations support the theoretical predictions and demonstrate accurate implementation of virtual cooling with reduced resource requirements. Our results establish VAP as a resource-efficient and scalable approach to quantum-state purification in near-term devices.

title: Linear-mode photon counting performance and intrinsic dark current in HgCdTe APDs for quantum optical applications
summary: The performance of HgCdTe APDs for single photon detection at T=80 K has been characterized using a hybrized Resistive Trans-Impedance Amplifier (RTIA) and a deported Capacitance Trans-impedance amplifier (CTIA). The single-photon detection capacity was characterized with the HgCdTe APDs operated in linear mode with high APD gain, M>400, and hybridized with the RTIA. The measurements revealed an external photon detection efficiency (PDE) of 42 % to 55 %, and a dark count rate (DCR) of 2.6 MHz to 17 MHz, for an amplitude threshold ranging from 2.5 to 4.5 times the rms noise of the amplifier. Taking into account the unity gain quantum efficiency, QE=63%, this corresponds to an internal PDE ranging from 66 % to 86 %. Using the deported CTIA, it was demonstrated that the high level of DCR is not the intrinsic limit of the APD technology. The CTIA approach enables direct measurement of the APD dark current, Idark, with gain-normalized dark current levels as low as Idark/M=10.9 fA at M = 450. This corresponds to a DCR of 150 Hz which is compatible with the requirements for most of the quantum photonics applications.

title: Bound entanglement as a trigonometric moment problem
summary: Entangled states that are positive under partial transposition (PPT) are the main obstruction to a simple description of entanglement. We study three basic questions about them within a class of multiqubit states, the mixtures, with real but possibly negative weights, of products of equatorial spin coherent states of several groups of qubits: which PPT entangled states belong to the class, how robust their entanglement is to white noise, and how small their rank can be. In this class each question becomes a question about a truncated trigonometric moment problem. Every such state is PPT across every bipartition, and it is fully separable exactly when an associated multi-level Toeplitz matrix is the moment matrix of a positive measure on the torus. We answer the three questions exactly in the following cases. For three qubits, every rank-four PPT entangled state with nonzero Lorentz invariant belongs to the class after invertible local operators, which proves a working hypothesis of Garberg, Irgens and Myrheim and yields a complete set of invariants for this seven-dimensional family; among the states with vanishing invariant, exactly a one-parameter family belongs to it. For every three-qubit state built from an unextendible product basis, the white-noise threshold for full separability is $λ^*=1-2/(1+\sqrt{1+s})$ with a local-unitary invariant $s\in(0,1]$, and $λ^*=3-2\sqrt2$ for the Shifts basis; a witness in closed form detects every entangled state of this family with eight local Pauli settings. For two groups of qubits we construct extremal states of minimal rank, and for three groups we determine the minimal rank of entanglement within the class in several configurations.

title: From BBM92 Measurements to Secure Keys: Challenges in a Practical Implementation
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures. Published in Entropy Special Issue "Quantum Information" Celebrating Professor Gilles Brassard's 70th Birthday
summary: The protocol introduced by C. H. Bennett, G. Brassard and N. D. Mermin in 1992 (BBM92) is one of the most important and widely adopted quantum key distribution (QKD) protocols. As with any other QKD protocol, its practical security depends on satisfying the assumptions underlying its theoretical security proofs. Here, we examine two common implementations of BBM92: a conventional passive receiver and a time-multiplexed configuration that halves the number of detectors. We characterise the passive polarisation analysers common to both architectures and present experimental results obtained with the time-multiplexed receiver, employing a continuous-wave (CW) pumped spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC) source of polarisation-entangled photon pairs and threshold detectors. We investigate the challenges encountered during post-processing when attempting to satisfy the requirements of existing security proofs and discuss the gap between theoretical security assumptions and the extraction of a provably secure cryptographic key.

title: Sharp rank thresholds and cubic support in PPT extensions of completely symmetric states
summary: For completely symmetric states on $d\ge3$ parties of actual local rank $N\ge3$, the least rank of an entangled state passing any prescribed finite positive level of the PPT extension hierarchy is $3d+N-3$. At equality, the two- and three-party marginals recover a ternary plane cubic shared by every extension. On this cubic the hierarchy becomes exact at a finite level precisely when every singularity outside the zero locus of the contraction quadratic is a split real node. We give the first exact level or an exact feasibility test for it, independent of $d$. On a smooth cubic the thresholds along the specified paths to the square of a flex tangent reduce to elliptic division and have unique rank-two Gram matrices. On reflection-invariant paths we obtain a quartic formula and the leading asymptotic constant. The least rank for entanglement itself is $3d+N-5$, and we classify equality. An explicit rational rank-nine three-qutrit state on a smooth cubic passes the first extension level and fails the second.

title: A Relativistic Quantum Mechanical Formulation of Wu-Shaknov Entanglements
comment: Some further improvements upon the text have been made
summary: It is suggested that a spontaneous formation of quantum mechanical entanglements does actually occur between spin, helicity and polarization states involved in creation-annihilation processes. A framework built up earlier that presumably affords a unified relativistic quantum mechanical description of free particle-antiparticle pairs of any spin is used to propose a comprehensive formulation of Wu-Shaknov entanglements. Explicit relationships between amplitudes and Born-like probabilities associated to incoming and outgoing states are obtained thereafter on the basis of certain theoretical assumptions. The behaviours of these relationships under the action of a dynamical group which is taken to supply observational correlations for different frames in spacetime are then specified. It appears that a modified version of some of the conventional conservation laws may afford a set of general selection rules for the formation of relativistic entanglements.

title: On a local hidden-variable model for postselected EPR correlations
summary: A theoretical and numerical analysis of a Bell-type experiment is presented, where linear polarization measurements on nonmaximally entangled two-qubit states are modeled through a sigmoid-based threshold mechanism that violates the fair-sampling assumption required by the CHSH inequality. Numerical simulations characterize how closely this local construction can reproduce quantum-like correlations in the postselected detected sample, for both the |Phi_r> and |Psi_r> states over a range of entanglement parameters. For the tested configurations, the model produces CHSH-type violations only in the postselected detected sample through a setting-dependent detection mechanism, operating outside the assumptions of both the CHSH inequality and Mermin's 82.8% efficiency bound. The model is not in conflict with loophole-free Bell experiments, which specifically close the detection loophole exploited here. The CH--Eberhard analysis in the one-detector-per-side configuration yields J < 0 throughout the full range of entanglement parameters, as required for a strictly local model. The model is further extended with a local adaptive-threshold mechanism implementing one-sided memory. A paired comparison shows that this specific memory rule produces a systematic and reproducible shift in the CH--Eberhard parameter J relative to the fixed-threshold model, while leaving the CH--Eberhard analysis qualitatively unchanged under the tested conditions. The results characterize how a local, setting-dependent postselection mechanism shapes Bell-test statistics across a range of entanglement parameters, within the specific configurations and threshold rules tested.

title: Gutzwiller Quantum-Classical Embedding for Dynamics Simulations of Correlated Electron Systems
summary: Simulating the real-time dynamics of correlated electron systems requires a nonperturbative treatment of local correlations over long times, a challenge for classical methods. We present the time-dependent Gutzwiller quantum-classical embedding framework, t-GQCE, for generic multi-orbital lattice models with time-dependent Hamiltonians. Within the time-dependent ghost Gutzwiller approximation, the lattice dynamics is mapped onto a noninteracting quasiparticle lattice, propagated classically, coupled to finite interacting embedding models propagated on quantum processors. The two parts exchange only embedding Hamiltonian parameters and single-particle density matrices, and the framework is agnostic to the quantum dynamics solver. We demonstrate it with adaptive variational quantum dynamics simulations of interaction quenches in the Hubbard model on the Bethe lattice. Without ghost orbitals, the embedding problem reduces to a single qubit, simulated on IBM quantum hardware with two qubits, including an ancilla. With more ghost orbitals, t-GQCE suppresses the artificial undamped oscillations of the conventional Gutzwiller approximation and approaches nonequilibrium dynamical mean-field theory results for weak and strong quenches. Statevector simulations with 2, 4 and 6 ghost orbitals per spin, or 8, 12 and 16 qubits, give adaptive circuits that follow the embedding states with infidelities below $5\times10^{-4}$. Under trapped-ion noise models, circuit compression, measurements in rotated orbital bases with post-selection, and noise mitigation reduce the measurement errors severalfold. At one third of the error rates of a hardware-benchmarked noise model, they reach an accuracy of $0.01$ for the single-particle density matrix and the double occupancy with $10^5$ shots per time step, and the Quantinuum H2-Emulator gives similar accuracy.

title: No-Go Theorems for Ordered Universal Entanglement Purification
summary: Entanglement purification is a fundamental tool for obtaining high-fidelity entangled states used in various quantum technologies. It aims to increase the fidelity of noisy shared entangled states with a fixed maximally entangled state through LOCC. In distributed quantum systems, such as networks employing quantum repeaters, limited memory, probabilistic entanglement generation, and unequal storage times can leave a finite collection of nonidentical pairs. Their states may remain incompletely characterized even when calibrated preparation and storage records establish their fidelity ordering. Recent work has investigated whether fidelity ordering permits nontrivial universal purification. A nontrivial universal $n$-to-1 protocol must, conditioned on success, never lower the highest input fidelity and strictly increase it for at least one allowed joint input. Although no-go results have been established for a restricted class of LOCC protocols, the corresponding question for general LOCC has remained unresolved. Here, we study ordered universal purification under separable operations.
